source_neutral.procedure: Observe one approval workflow over time as a sequence of handoff stages. Obtain the actual stages and owners from the workflow map; illustrative stage names do not establish the workflow. In each run, change one input at one handoff: either the release rate of a defined request class or one bounded process setting, such as review cadence, the number of authorized approvers, or the threshold below which a request skips a stage. Apply a known change abruptly at a recorded time and hold it constant. Track stage queues, waiting times, completions and end-to-end turnaround from a recorded pre-change period through the response. Assess where delay accumulates and which tested changes qualify as candidate remedies, conditional on the starting conditions and conditions during the run.
source_neutral.action: Choose one input and one handoff. Set the change amount in advance, large enough for its response to be distinguishable from pre-change day-to-day variation and small enough to remain within service-level targets and staff capacity. Predetermine the sampling interval, the band defining sufficient proximity to a stable level, the required number of consecutive intervals within that band, the minimum observation window and the abort thresholds. Set the minimum window to several multiples of the longest stage cycle observed before the change, including any batch or meeting cycle. Record initial queue lengths, in-flight items, staffing and demand during the pre-change period. Apply the entire change at the recorded time and hold it constant, making no other deliberate changes during the run. At every sampling interval, record queue length, waiting time and completions for every stage from the changed handoff downstream, together with end-to-end turnaround. Maintain these records from the pre-change period through the response. In parallel, log staffing, incoming demand, case mix, calendar events and any other process changes.
source_neutral.observables: Compute per-stage queue length, waiting time from queue entry to pickup, completions per interval and end-to-end turnaround from ticket timestamps at the fixed sampling interval, which may be a working day. For each stage, record the interval between the input change and the first output change distinguishable from pre-change variation, and the order in which stages begin responding. Measure how quickly queue length, waiting time or completion rate approaches its new level. Record whether queue length or turnaround temporarily exceeds its eventual level, including the height and timing of the maximum; one possible sequence is an increased upstream release followed by a downstream queue increase. Identify repeated queue growth and reduction, and compare its period with known review-meeting or batch-release cycles. Measure the time until an output remains within the preset stability band. Calculate differences between pre-change and stable levels of queue length, waiting time, completion rate and end-to-end turnaround. Record queues that continue growing without stabilizing, outputs that stop changing after reaching a maximum, and any absence of distinguishable change at a stage or in end-to-end turnaround.
source_neutral.inferential_warrant: Treat observations as constraints on candidate explanations, without identifying a unique explanation. A long interval before a detectable response followed by a prompt change suggests fixed waiting, such as scheduled review, batch release or transfer latency, rather than insufficient processing capacity. Continued queue growth without stabilization after an intake increase suggests that the stage is capacity-limited at the tested load and accumulates delay. A slow approach to a new level and a long time to stabilize suggest a large backlog through which the change takes effect, delaying end-to-end improvement. Repeated queue growth and reduction with a period matching a meeting or batch cycle suggests batching. Such repetition without a matching cycle, or with items returning to earlier stages, suggests rework or escalation involving repeated stage visits. A temporary downstream increase above the eventual level after an upstream change suggests that delay moves to another stage rather than being removed. For a process-setting change, the difference between pre-change and stable turnaround estimates the effect of that bounded change under the tested conditions. A local improvement without an end-to-end change suggests that another handoff determines the remaining delay. Identify delay accumulation at stages with the longest interval before a detectable response, queues that fail to stabilize, or the longest time to stabilize. A bounded change qualifies as a candidate remedy when it produces a stable reduction in turnaround, no sustained downstream increase above the eventual level, a consistent response when reversed and a similar result on repetition. Every conclusion remains conditional on the tested change amount, direction, request class, demand and staffing. Interpret responses to the designed changes alongside the associations from timestamp and queue comparisons; those comparisons remain part of the assessment.
source_neutral.problem_decomposition: Use one workflow as the overall unit, with mapped stages and accountable owners as its component units. Locate each intervention at one handoff and vary one input per run. Distinguish request release rate from process settings. Track the changed handoff and every downstream stage separately while relating their response order, queues, waiting times and completion rates to end-to-end turnaround. Account for requests already queued or in flight at the start, informal queues that may be unrecorded, and request-class differences. Relevant relationships include downstream effects of upstream releases, scheduled batch or meeting cycles, returns to earlier stages, shared approvers and staffing adjustments that connect multiple stages. Compare runs across change amounts, directions, handoffs, demand levels and staffing levels while retaining the conditions specific to each run.
source_neutral.next_inquiry: Reverse the change and record the return over time to check whether responses in opposite directions are symmetric. Repeat with a different change amount and at a different demand or staffing level. Repeat at other handoffs, changing one input at a time. Compare the results with timestamp comparisons, exception-case reviews and interviews. If a major logged disturbance overlaps the response period, mark the run and repeat it under comparable demand and staffing. Causal attribution of a remedy requires repetition under comparable demand and staffing.
source_neutral.limits: Before acting, verify these assumptions: stage timestamps exist and reflect actual work movement rather than logging time; the chosen input can be changed abruptly at a known time by a known amount and then held constant; a recorded pre-change period documents initial queues, in-flight items, staffing and demand without presuming a stable starting state; and those accountable for the workflow authorize the change, its amount and its abort thresholds. End observation as stabilized when outputs have remained within the preset band for the required consecutive intervals and the minimum observation window has elapsed. Abort if a service-level threshold is breached or a queue continues growing beyond its limit; reverse the change and retain the record as evidence of a reached capacity or response limit, or failure to stabilize, under the tested conditions. Mark a run as affected by a disturbance when a major logged disturbance overlaps the response period, and repeat under comparable demand and staffing. Low case volumes make per-interval queue counts and waiting times coarse and variable; mixed case types obscure response features, and small changes may be indistinguishable from pre-change variation. Existing backlog, in-flight work and unlogged informal queues can make early responses reflect prior history. Fully loaded approvers, working-hour limits and service-level caps can prevent further output change and conceal how the workflow responds. People may reprioritize, expedite or work differently when a change is announced or observed; effects of large changes need not scale from small changes, and increases and decreases may produce different responses. Demand swings, absences, period-end peaks, holidays and policy changes may mimic or obscure response features. Shared approvers, concurrent initiatives and staffing adjustments made in response to the intervention confound attribution to the chosen input. Ending observation before slow stages or long batch cycles complete understates stabilization time and misstates the difference between pre-change and stable levels. Results at the tested demand, staffing and case mix may not apply at peak load or to other request classes. An abrupt change may be infeasible because implementation is gradual or anticipated. Organizational changes during a run may alter the workflow being assessed. Ethical and service obligations constrain change size. A single run provides one observed instance, and conclusions may not generalize beyond the tested change.
